papers.title: The Role of Sycophancy in Confidence Calibration When Offloading Memory and Judgement Processes to AI
papers.summary: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday life is reshaping how people approach cognitive tasks. However, inappropriate reliance remains a barrier to synergistic team performance, with human-AI teams often failing to outperform the best of either agent alone (Vaccaro et al., 2024). Effective human-AI collaboration requires accurate mental models of the distributed cognitive system. That is, individuals must have an awareness of both the capabilities of AI system and their own cognitive limitations, in order to discern whether to accept or reject AI advice. While considerable research has looked at system-level factors, focusing on improving the users’ understanding of AI behaviour to foster appropriate reliance (e.g., XAI), less attention has been given to individual-level cognitive factors in augmented decision making, such as how humans monitor and evaluate their own cognition. Such metacognitive evaluations predict cognitive offloading strategies, with underconfidence driving automation bias (Ma et al., 2024). However, the reverse relationship—how reliance on external tools shapes metacognition—remains poorly understood. There is emerging evidence that partnering with AI systems inflates confidence such that metacognitive evaluations no longer align with actual performance, resulting in metacognitive miscalibration (Fernandes et al., 2026; Taudien e

papers.title: From the fluency fallacy to the micro-to-macro validity gap: opportunities and pitfalls of LLMs in social simulation
papers.summary: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into social simulation has generated considerable enthusiasm, but also raises substantial methodological and epistemological challenges. This critical review examines the use of LLMs as cognitive or decision-making components of simulated agents from a computational social science perspective. Rather than treating the psychological evaluation of LLMs as separate from simulation mechanics, we argue that their behavioral and epistemic limitations can become systemic vulnerabilities when scaled to multi-agent societies. We first map the rapidly evolving landscape of LLM-driven platforms, ranging from small narrative sandboxes to population-scale and spatially structured simulations. We then develop a unified critical framework for analyzing the Micro-to-Macro Validity Gap: the propagation, nonlinear amplification, or convergent contraction of micro-level limitations—including hallucinations, stochastic inconsistency, representational biases, and alignment effects—into agent-level distortions (such as average persona convergence) and macro-level risks (such as artificial consensus and behavioral homogenization), while exposing evaluators to epistemic vulnerabilities such as the Fluency Fallacy and automation bias. We identify contexts in which LLM-based agents offer genuine operational value, including serious games, participatory env

papers.title: AgentMesh: Toward Redundancy- and Barrier-Free Dataflow in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) now power long-running agentic applications like deep research and coding agents, yet their end-to-end latency reaches minutes to hours. The runtime executes each dataflow as an opaque, indivisible block at coarse granularity, wasting end-to-end time on redundancy (acquiring content already held or unnecessary) and barriers (a downstream component idling until its upstream input is entirely ready). We abstract a produce–transfer–consume dataflow as a basic unit in MAS, where the producer is a tool or LLM decoding, and the consumer is an LLM prefill. We present AgentMesh, a MAS runtime that optimizes each dataflow with three mechanisms: Delta Tool Retrieval (DTR) shrinks the produce step by serving a tool result’s cached items and fetching only the semantic delta; Branch-Parallel Prefill (BPP) shrinks the consume step by prefilling independent branches in parallel under dependency-graph-derived attention sparsity; Dynamic-Equilibrium Streaming (DES), a dynamic pipeline, overlaps produce, transfer, and consume by pacing streamed chunks to the runtime rate of producer and consumer. Implemented on AutoGen, OpenCode, and vLLM and evaluated across three GPU generations and six models, AgentMesh reduces end-to-end latency by up to 62% with no statistically significant quality loss, on both deep research and coding agent workloads.

papers.title: FAAB: A Benchmark for Fault Detection and Responsibility Attribution in Financial Multi-Agent Workflows
papers.summary: Financial multi-agent systems distribute evidence extraction, expectation retrieval, consistency checking, decision, and settlement across roles. When a final claim is wrong, outcome accuracy cannot say where the evidence chain first broke or which role was responsible. We formulate financial multi-agent workflow auditing : given a typed workflow trace, detect whether a fault occurred, classify its root cause, and localize the earliest responsible agent and step. We introduce the Financial Agent Audit Benchmark (FAAB) for that task, built from 300 real point-in-time SEC and I/B/E/S workflows and pairing 300 untouched clean controls with 700 minimal single-point interventions over 14 fault classes spanning evidence, financial semantics, time, coordination, and settlement. Expert executable contracts detect every controlled fault at a zero clean false-positive rate and localize every responsible role and step, at no inference cost. A single-call LLM judge and a three-call debate reading the identical trace are substantially less reliable, particularly on clean-workflow calibration and causal localization. Capability alone does not close that gap in the useful direction. Across three models from two vendors, stronger free-form judges buy root causes with clean work: root-cause accuracy rises from 38.9% to 83.4% while clean false positives rise from 7.5% to 15.4%. papers.title: The triadic convergence in Industry 5.0: Orchestrating resilient supply chains, agile project management, and algorithmic Islamic banking through smart contracts and green sukuk
papers.summary: Contemporary global value networks and capital-intensive infrastructure projects face an existential crisis driven by geopolitical disruptions, persistent inflation, and the fragile leverage of conventional interest-based debt. Although Supply Chain Management (SCM), Project Management (PM), and Islamic Banking (IB) have evolved rapidly in isolation, a unified framework integrating all three is absent. This article bridges that gap by formulating the Triadic Convergence Framework (TCF), a novel cyber-physical-financial architecture operating within the human-centric and sustainable ethos of Industry 5.0. Grounded in Transaction Cost Economics, Agency Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and the socio-ethical axioms of Maqasid al-Shariah, this study employs a multi-layered conceptual and mathematical modeling approach. It synthesizes Q1 literature across artificial intelligence, blockchain-enabled Supply Chain Finance, Agile-Hybrid Project Management, and Islamic Sustainable Finance. Furthermore, it formulates a deterministic mathematical model linking Earned Value Management indices with automated, smart-contract-driven Islamic financing disbursements (Parallel Istisna’a and Tokenized Murabaha) verified by IoT Digital Twins. The integration of AI-driven Digital Twins and permissioned blockchain ledgers resolves the historical operational bottleneck of Islamic banking: the high

papers.title: The design and impact of a dual-agent artificial intelligence system in personalised mathematics tutoring
papers.summary: Digital tutoring tools are increasingly used in schools to support mathematics learning, but empirical evidence remains limited on how diagnostic and instructional functions can be coordinated to provide personalised support. This study examined a dual-agent intervention in which a diagnostic agent generated provisional learning-profile classifications (diverging, assimilating, converging, and accommodating) and a personalised tutoring agent delivered profile-responsive, stage-specific guidance within Polya’s (1945) problem-solving framework; a general tutoring agent provided non-profile-responsive guidance in the control condition. The quasi-experimental study involved 206 Chinese grade 5 students, including 99 in the experimental group and 107 in the control group. The pre-test and post-test used two parallel mathematics tasks evaluated using the same analytic rubric, and learning gain was calculated from these matched assessment components. The experimental group achieved a significantly larger mean gain than the control group (5.14 vs. 0.94, t(204) = 4.36, p < .001, Hedges’ g = .61). A baseline-adjusted sensitivity analysis confirmed the overall group effect (p < .001). After Holm correction for four profile-specific comparisons, only the assimilating-profile contrast remained significant (adjusted p = .0496). However, the omnibus group-by-profile interaction was not signif

papers.title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human–Agent Interfaces
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into applications, allowing users to complete tasks either through direct manipulation or by delegating actions to conversational agents. However, little is known about how users balance these modalities when both are available. We present a web-based content management system augmented with an LLM agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling users to perform CRUD tasks through a graphical interface, a conversational agent, or both. We conducted a between-subjects study (N=73) comparing three interaction modes: Traditional-Only, AI-First, and Hybrid. Across sixteen scenarios, we analyzed task completion time, interaction logs, and delegation behavior. AI-assisted interaction significantly reduced clicks, page navigations, and scrolling, indicating lower interaction effort. Surprisingly, these reductions did not translate into faster task completion, as task duration did not differ significantly across conditions. We also found no significant relationship between CRUD operation type and delegation, suggesting that users did not systematically avoid delegating higher-risk actions. Instead, delegation varied far more between participants than between tasks, with individual differences accounting for roughly half the variance in assistant use (ICC =.50). Our findings suggest that the primary benefit of human–agent i

papers.title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder: pathogenesis, epidemiological characteristics, animal models, and potential therapeutic strategies
papers.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a complex neurobehavioral disorder that disproportionately affects military service members. The clinical presentation of PTSD is heterogeneous and may overlap with other psychiatric conditions. According to the Fifth Edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), common symptoms include memory loss, mood and personality changes, impulsiveness, aggression, anxiety, and depression. The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying PTSD remain incompletely understood, although research implicates pathways involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, dysfunctional neural circuitry, neurochemical imbalances, neuroinflammatory processes, and genetic and epigenetic factors. Approximately 7% of the U.S. adult population has met the diagnostic criteria for PTSD in their lifetime, with a substantially higher prevalence of 12%-30% among military personnel. Multiple animal models, including single-stressor, intermediate complexity, social interaction, predator stress, and blast exposure paradigms, have been employed to investigate PTSD mechanisms. Current treatment strategies typically integrate pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy. Military service members are at increased risk for blast injuries, which frequently result in traumatic brain injury (TBI). Although some symptoms of TBI may resolve, approximately 20%

papers.title: Can TDD improve the quality of LLM-migrated code? : A pilot study in an industrial context
papers.summary: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLM) has created new possibilities for automating software development, yet ensuring the quality of AI-generated code remains a major challenge. We aim to investigate if Test-Driven Development (TDD) can improve the quality of code generated by an LLM in a fully autonomous context, within a pilot project at Decerno AB. We added TDD to their pilot workflow, using a design science approach, with continuous refinements to prompt design and workflow structure, based on observed AI behavior. The generated code was evaluated and compared with non-TDD code, using SonarQube for static code analysis. The results indicate that TDD reduced complexity and code duplication, but introduced more quality issues overall, while non-TDD produced fewer, but more severe issues. The generated tests from the TDD workflow focused more on content verification than on behavioral testing, contributing to a lower code coverage per test compared to non-TDD. The findings suggest that TDD involves trade-offs that may favor certain development priorities, in particular where lower complexity and reduced duplication are more beneficial than minimizing total issue count. This indicates that a strict application of TDD may not be optimal in an autonomous AI-driven context, and that exploring more flexible adaptations of the TDD workflow remains interesting for future resea

papers.title: From Coding to Creativity: Integrating Design Thinking into IT and Technology Education
papers.summary: This study examines how the integration of Design Thinking into Information Technology (IT) and technology education can bridge technical programming skills and creative, human-centered problem-solving. Specifically, it explores how the five stages of Design Thinking empathizing, defining, ideating, prototyping, and testing shape students’ creative thinking, active engagement, and collaborative learning experiences. A qualitative research approach was employed, involving teachers, students, and school principals as key informants. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, classroom observations, and documentation of learning activities, then analyzed thematically to identify recurring patterns in teaching practices and student experiences. The findings indicate that Design Thinking creates opportunities for students to move beyond coding procedures toward developing digital solutions that respond to real users’ needs. Through collaborative ideation, iterative prototyping, and feedback-based testing, students demonstrate greater involvement in learning, explore alternative solutions, and communicate their ideas more actively. The approach also provides opportunities to develop empathy, creativity, collaboration, and a willingness to experiment with and revise initial designs. papers.title: EgoPlay: Event-Triggered Video Editing for Egocentric Streams
papers.summary: We introduce EgoPlay, an event-triggered video-to-video editor for egocentric streams, obtained by fine-tuning a pretrained V2V diffusion transformer on event-conditioned data built primarily from Ego4D. Given a monocular video and an event-triggered prompt of the form "when X happens, do Y," EgoPlay infers whether and when event X occurs, preserves pre-event frames, and applies edit Y only to the post-event continuation. Rather than cascading a separate event detector with an editor, EgoPlay learns event recognition, temporal restraint, and pixel-level editing jointly in a single end-to-end model, while also handling negative and multi-event prompts. To support this, we construct a large-scale dataset of 106K event-triggered clip-prompt pairs spanning positive triggers, fabricated-trigger negatives, and multi-event prompts. We then train a bidirectional video diffusion editor with event-triggered supervision and derive a causal variant for chunk-by-chunk streamable inference. We further introduce an event-aware evaluation protocol that separately measures post-trigger editing quality, pre-trigger preservation, and false-trigger robustness. On the Ego4D benchmark, EgoPlay substantially outperforms EgoEdit, the state-of-the-art instruction-based egocentric video editing baseline, with relative gains of 17.7%, 16.9%, and 16.4% in editing quality, visual quality, and background co

papers.title: GLOSS: Geometric Local Self-Similarity Learning for Faithful Reference-Guided Texture Fill
papers.summary: Using conditional image generators, texture artists can explore many single-view looks for an existing 3D shape. Despite impressive progress, state-of-the-art generative methods still struggle to generate a full object texture while closely adhering to fine scale geometric detail and single view references, leaving little room for artists guidance. Furthermore, current automatic models lack the flexibility for artist to explore multiple textures from varied sources in an interactive and controllable manner. Unlike methods trained on large 3D datasets that generate full object textures from global guidance, our work explores a local and less data-hungry approach to texture with explicit artist control. We leverage the geometric self-similarity and geometry-texture correlation existing in many natural and man-made shapes; and train a shape-specific local texture generation and completion model. This model learns from existing image model priors and a single 3D shape, and is guided by attending to a set of geometry-aware reference patches. The trained shape-specific network can transfer any novel reference to the full target object texture through patchwise inpainting. We show improved or comparable quality to strong image-conditioned texture generation baselines, suggesting local texturing as a promising research direction. Our model also enables local geometry-conditioned textur

papers.title: InstantMimic: A High Performance System for Learning Physics-based Skills in Seconds
papers.summary: Physics-based character control is a long-standing challenge in computer graphics and robotics, requiring policies that satisfy complex dynamics while producing realistic motion. Recent Deep RL approaches, particularly imitation learning methods such as DeepMimic, have had broad impact beyond animation, influencing robotics by enabling agile and expressive behaviors. While these approaches achieve impressive results, they remain computationally inefficient to train in practice. Despite GPU-accelerated simulation, we find that end-to-end pipelines often underutilize hardware due to overheads outside the physics solver, caused by fragmented GPU kernels and CPU memory access in the critical path. We present InstantMimic, a system that addresses these inefficiencies by making the entire training loop GPU-native. Built on a GPU-native physics backend, our unified pipeline integrates simulation, environment computation, policy inference, and policy updates within a single execution flow. As a result, InstantMimic reduces training time for diverse physics-based skills to a few seconds and makes LLM-agent-driven hyperparameter search practical.

papers.title: Nonpredictive approaches in marketing
papers.summary: Abstract Much academic research is focused on the application of predictive data, forecasts, and models to inform practical marketing decision-making. Such work offers powerful insights to marketers directing their firms and interacting with the environments in which they operate. The present study is devoted to the smaller, alternative, and equally potent body of work that seeks to enable decision-making without reliance on prediction. We term this category of approaches ‘nonpredictive’ because their operative basis for action does not depend on prior estimation of future states or outcomes. Instead, decision paths are generated and revised through mechanisms of action, interaction, commitment, recombination, experimentation, and imagined direction. This foundation enables nonpredictive approaches to function across a wide variety of marketing decisions, including truly uncertain situations where prediction cannot reliably guide action. Interest in nonpredictive approaches is emerging but has yet to be consolidated. We inventory and synthesize nonpredictive approaches in the marketing literature, contributing to academic discussion at the foundation of marketing decision-making. In the process, we clarify conceptual specifics of nonpredictive approaches, construct a taxonomy that distinguishes among them, and develop a series of propositions to inform future research. papers.title: CliniCIRCA: LLM-powered Clinical Timeline Generation and Summarization from Unstructured EHR Texts for Mental Health Patients
papers.summary: Abstract Background: Mental health care often requires clinicians to reason over patient journeys: longitudinal patterns of symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, behaviors, social context, and responses to care. Yet these journeys are rarely documented as readily available, explicit timelines. Clinically important temporal information is often embedded in unstructured discharge narratives, where events may be repeated, narrated out of order, or expressed through vague and relative time references. This makes temporal recovery difficult for clinicians and computational systems, and can limit the reliability of downstream summarization. Methods: We present CliniCIRCA, a multi-stage large language model (LLM) framework for Calendar-anchored, Imprecision-aware Reconstruction of Clinical Annals. CliniCIRCA decomposes patient-journey reconstruction into three stages: extracting atomic clinical events from raw discharge summaries, assigning calendar-grounded temporal labels with explicit uncertainty, and rendering the verified timeline as a date-grouped clinical summary. The framework is designed to make temporal reasoning inspectable rather than hidden inside a single summarization step. Results: From 14,882 MIMIC-III mental-health-coded admissions, we construct a benchmark of 52 discharge summaries on which CliniCIRCA produces 15,891 temporally tagged events. papers.title: Robotic search and rescue in earthquake-collapsed buildings: capabilities, evidence gaps, and a roadmap for human-multi-robot rescue
papers.summary: Following an earthquake, rescue robots must search for and assist trapped individuals in complex environments characterized by unstable rubble, narrow cavities, darkness, dust, and unreliable communications. This paper reviews the technical evidence for seven categories of robots within the seven-stage mission chain of search and rescue (SAR) in building collapse scenarios, covering unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs); tracked, wheeled, and reconfigurable robots; quadrupedal robots; snake-like and continuum robots; humanoid and hybrid robots; heavy-duty engineering robots; and casualty evacuation and medical transport robots. This paper evaluates representative “platform-sensor-mission” capabilities across two independent dimensions: validation maturity (E0–E4) and relevance to collapse rescue scenarios (S0–S4). The study clearly distinguishes between signals indicating the possible presence of trapped individuals, 3D positioning information usable to guide excavation operations, and the actual execution of subsequent rescue operations. Currently, evidence of field applications is primarily concentrated on tasks such as site entry, reconnaissance, mapping, visual search, and the detection of vital signs through rubble. In contrast, evidence regarding sustained communication, supply delivery, close-range manipulation of casualties, casualty management, evacuation, and mission handof

papers.title: Teachers as architects of self-regulated learning: a systematic review of teacher practices for fostering self-regulated learning environments
papers.summary: This systematic review synthesizes empirical research on teacher practices intended to support self-regulated learning (SRL) in K-12 education, including general and inclusive settings. Following PRISMA guidelines, 47 studies published between 2000 and 2026 were examined to map instructional practices, research methods, and educational contexts. The findings identify both direct and indirect approaches to SRL support, including explicit strategy instruction, goal setting, feedback, self-monitoring, reflection and self-assessment, student choice, collaborative learning, and supportive teacher–student interactions. These practices were examined in relation to the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases of Zimmerman’s cyclical model, as well as co-regulation and socially shared regulation. The review also highlights the role of technology-supported instruction while indicating that evidence remains limited in secondary and inclusive educational settings. Importantly, the findings distinguish practices reported or implemented in classrooms from evidence of changes in students’ regulatory processes or academic outcomes; the effectiveness of practices should, therefore, be interpreted in light of study design and methodological quality. The review provides a descriptive synthesis of teacher practices investigated in empirical research and identifies priorities for future

papers.title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly ‘reason’ with increasing sophistication, but whether they ‘know’ when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning–Kruger–like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence–accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning syst

papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: An Assessment of Accessibility and Affordability of Inpatient Psychiatric Care in Tennessee
papers.summary: Introduction: Access to mental health has seen changes over the past decade, but little research and attention have been given to access to inpatient psychiatric facilities. Inpatient psychiatric care is crucial for patients experiencing mental health emergencies who need immediate access to care. Gaps in spatial accessibility, affordability, and the access and assessment process were identified due to a lack of available information in the field. Methods: Secondary data from the Tennessee Department of Health were used to assess financial accessibility through payer source charges and patient encounters, as well as through mapping of inpatient psychiatric facilities and conducting drive time and coverage area analyses. Primary data were collected through interviews with clinicians located in Northeastern Tennessee to gain insight into the assessment process and gather their perceptions of inpatient care. Results: Longitudinal descriptive reviews on the financial accessibility among Tennessee Inpatient Facilities. This showed increased variability among facilities when stratified by region, ownership, and type of operation. Spatial accessibility in ArcGIS showed 82% of counties were not covered within a 30-minute radius of inpatient facilities. Analysis showed that Middle Tennessee had significantly less coverage from inpatient facilities and raised concerns about spatial-socia

papers.title: Pieces Solving a Puzzle: Emerging Roles and Cross-Field Analogies During a Distributed Epistemic Game
papers.summary: In an effort to describe why some problems can’t be solved, a character compared them to a cubic meter of platinum - a block so dense that all the people who could squeeze around it still couldn’t lift it off the ground. In the same way, these problems simply can’t have enough people gathered around and communicating about them - and so they remain unsolved. This research looks at the first Polymath Project (2009) as an example of a distributed epistemic game to examine how groups engage with complex problems. and without a locally omniscient individual. In this setting of epistemic uncertainty, interactions between individuals reveal patterns of participation, and an analogy opens a new solution pathway by introducing a problem-solving approach from another field. These insights answer the initial question of the Polymath Project - ‘Is massively collaborative mathematics possible?’ - and offer hope for lifting the cubic meter of other unsolvable problems.

papers.title: Sex-Dependent Modulation of the Endocannabinoid System in Pain Processing
papers.summary: Medical cannabis, also known as medical marijuana, is becoming a more popular treatment for many diseases, including chronic pain. Chronic pain is difficult to treat, and current pain relievers are less effective in women. Medical cannabis may be a useful alternative to the medications that are currently available, but more research is needed to determine how safe and effective it is. Cannabis belongs to a class of drugs known as cannabinoids, which act on the body’s own endocannabinoid system to produce its effects. Cannabinoids affect the sexes differently, but it is not clear what causes these differences. Our research explored how sex hormones like estrogen and testosterone affect the efficacy of cannabinoids. To do this, I first examined whether removing these hormones would affect the brain’s response to THC, the main ingredient in cannabis. I found that THC affected brain regions differently in mice with depleted hormones. Additionally, THC affected brain regions differently in males and females. Next, I tested whether testosterone and estrogen affected how well cannabinoids worked as pain relievers. I found that testosterone reduced the drug’s efficacy in females, while estrogens reduced its efficacy in males. This would suggest that hormones have a different effect on males and females, leading to differences in the cannabinoid’s pain-relieving ability. Lastly, I sough

papers.title: Recent Advances in Medical Imaging Segmentation: Generative, Few-Shot, Foundation and Universal Models
papers.summary: Medical imaging is a cornerstone of modern healthcare, driving advancements in diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient care. Among its various tasks, segmentation remains one of the most challenging problems due to factors such as data accessibility, annotation complexity, structural variability, variation in medical imaging modalities, and privacy constraints. Despite recent progress, achieving robust generalization and domain adaptation remains a significant hurdle, particularly given the resource-intensive nature of some proposed models and their reliance on domain expertise. This survey explores cutting-edge advancements in medical image segmentation, focusing on methodologies such as Generative AI, Few-Shot Learning, Foundation Models, and Universal Models. These approaches offer promising solutions to longstanding challenges. We provide a comprehensive overview of the theoretical foundations, state-of-the-art techniques, and recent applications of these methods. Finally, we discuss inherent limitations, unresolved issues, and future research directions aimed at enhancing the practicality and accessibility of segmentation models in medical imaging. We maintain a GitHub Repository to continue tracking and updating innovations in this field.

papers.title: The World is Your Canvas: Painting Promptable Events with Reference Images, Trajectories, and Text
papers.summary: We present WorldCanvas, a framework for promptable world events that enables rich, user-directed simulation by combining text, trajectories, and reference images. Unlike text-only approaches and existing trajectory-controlled image-to-video methods, our multimodal approach combines trajectories -- encoding motion, timing, and visibility -- with natural language for semantic intent and reference images for visual grounding of object identity, enabling the generation of coherent, controllable events that include multi-agent interactions, object entry/exit, reference-guided appearance and counterintuitive events. The resulting videos demonstrate not only temporal coherence but also emergent consistency, preserving object identity and scene despite temporary disappearance. By supporting expressive world events generation, WorldCanvas advances world models from passive predictors to interactive, user-shaped simulators. Our project page is available at: https://worldcanvas.github.io/.

papers.title: Discovering High Level Patterns from Simulation Traces
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are unable to reliably reason about specific physical systems. Attempts to imbue LLMs with knowledge of the necessary physics concepts have shown great promise, but explainability and validation remain open challenges. An emerging alternative is tooling, where LLMs can query physical simulators and use the resulting simulation traces as context for validation. This approach suffers from poor scalability since simulation traces contain large volumes of fine-grained numerical and semantic data. We show that translating simulation traces to a sparse representation of "high-level" structural patterns leads to more effective interpretation by LLMs. We propose an unsupervised learning scheme to perform this translation, or annotation, via program synthesis. Our learning results in a library of programs that act as pattern detectors which can translate simulation traces to sparse, annotated pattern sequences. The detected patterns may optionally be guided by human experts via string labels (rigid collision, stretching spring, etc.). We show, using a recent physics benchmark, that such annotated representations are more amenable to natural language reasoning about specific physical systems. papers.title: DiCEGI Diversified Counterfactual Explanations for a Group of Instances
papers.summary: Machine learning techniques are now essential in many critical real-world domains to support decision-making. However, expert users often need explanations for the decisions made by these models. One key approach to explainable AI is using counterfactual explanations. These involve making small changes to input instances and observing how the machine learning model’s decision changes. For explaining outcomes for a group of instances, the explainer should identify a few diverse small interventions that are relevant to most of those instances rather than providing explanations for each one individually. In a classification setting that may involve multiple labels, we introduce a method called $$\text {DiCE}_{GI}$$ that relies on an augmented Lagrangian method to identify the optimal set of perturbations to apply collectively to a group of instances. Experiments conducted on both artificial and real datasets demonstrate that $$\text {DiCE}_{GI}$$ consistently returns the set of K interventions minimizing cost and maximizing coverage and diversity.
